title: The Bowling Scores of the Norton Street Gang
text:
In the late 1930s the young sociologist William Foote Whyte moved into the North End of Boston, a poor Italian American neighborhood he called Cornerville, and lived there for several years. He became friends with a group of young men who hung around a street corner and whom he called the Nortons. Their leader was a man he called Doc.

The Nortons often went bowling on Saturday nights, and bowling scores became a matter of pride. Whyte noticed a curious pattern. Over time, the members' scores tended to line up with their rank in the group. Doc and his close lieutenants usually bowled well, while low-status members did poorly, even when some of them were capable bowlers who performed much better when they played with others.

When a low-ranking member started to beat higher-ranking ones, the group heckled him and reminded him of his place, and his game soon fell apart. At a prize match the gang organized, the final standings came out almost exactly in the order of the group's hierarchy. Whyte concluded that confidence and performance were shaped by a person's position in the group and the expectations of the others.
lesson: How well people perform depends partly on where they stand in the group and what others expect of them. Leaders can lift or sink someone simply through their confidence in them.
source: Whyte, W. F. (1943). Street Corner Society: The Social Structure of an Italian Slum. University of Chicago Press.
caveat: It is an ethnography of one group described by a single observer, so it is a rich case rather than a measured result.
